title: Interactive Learning of Single-Index Models via Stochastic Gradient Descent
claim: Under adaptive data, SGD shows a slow burn-in phase followed by rapid learning, then converges to near-perfect alignment.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side; averaged curve with shaded band versus single trajectory
description: Two line plots sit side by side with the same axes: iteration t from 0 to 80000 on the x-axis, and correlation ⟨θ_t, θ*⟩ on the y-axis. The left panel (a) shows the mean over 100 runs as a blue curve on a light-blue shaded one-standard-deviation band. It rises slowly from about 0.22, climbs steeply between roughly 10k and 40k iterations, then flattens near 1.0, and the band narrows as it converges. The right panel (b) shows one noisy, jagged trajectory with the same S-shaped rise: a slow start, a rapid ascent, and a plateau near 1. Each panel has a small 'Correlation' legend and light gridlines. Captions under each panel describe the averaging and the single trajectory. The eye goes first to the left panel's shaded band.
caption: Correlation mt = ⟨θt, θ⋆⟩plotted as a function of t in d = 20 dimensions, for the cubic link f(x) = x3. We run interactive SGD with a constant learning rate ηt = 0.002 for all t, using an exploration schedule with σt = 0.5 until mt reaches 0.7 and σt = 0.2 thereafter.
abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a cornerstone algorithm for high-dimensional optimization, renowned for its empirical successes. Recent theoretical advances have provided a deep understanding of how SGD enables feature learning in high-dimensional nonlinear models, most notably the \textit{single-index model} with i.i.d. data. In this work, we study the sequential learning problem for single-index models, also known as generalized linear bandits or ridge bandits, where SGD is a simple and natural solution, yet its learning dynamics remain largely unexplored. We show that, similar to the optimal interactive learner, SGD undergoes a distinct ``burn-in'' phase before entering the ``learning'' phase in this setting. Moreover, with an appropriately chosen learning rate schedule, a single SGD procedure simultaneously achieves near-optimal (or best-known) sample complexity and regret guarantees across both phases, for a broad class of link functions. Our results demonstrate that SGD remains highly competitive for learning single-index models under adaptive data.
